# Searching by File Type in ripgrep

ripgrep has a built-in system for filtering search results to specific file types. This saves you from typing long glob patterns every time you want to narrow your search to particular kinds of files.

## What Are File Types?

A file type is a named category that corresponds to one or more filename patterns. For example, ripgrep's `rust` type includes the pattern `*.rs`. The `c` type includes both `*.c` and `*.h` files. Instead of writing out these patterns, you specify the file type name and ripgrep does the filtering for you.

ripgrep comes with dozens of built-in file types for common programming languages and document formats: `python`, `javascript`, `html`, `css`, `json`, `markdown`, `xml`, and many others. Each type is defined by a set of glob patterns that match files of that kind.

## Limiting Your Search to a File Type: `--type`

The `--type` flag tells ripgrep to search *only* files matching a particular type.

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
```

This searches for the pattern `fn run` but only in Rust source files (files matching `*.rs`). You can use the short form `-t` if you prefer:

```
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

Multiple `--type` flags can be combined. For example, to search only C or C++ files:

```
$ rg 'int main' -tc -tcpp
```

This is much easier than writing out the glob patterns yourself. Without `--type`, you'd have to remember all the extensions and quote them properly for your shell.

## Excluding a File Type: `--type-not`

The opposite of `--type` is `--type-not`. This tells ripgrep to search *every* file *except* those matching a particular type.

```
$ rg 'TODO' --type-not rust
```

This searches for the pattern `TODO` but skips all Rust files. The short form is `-T` (uppercase):

```
$ rg 'TODO' -Trust
```

You can combine multiple exclusions:

```
$ rg 'TODO' -Trust -Tpython
```

This searches everywhere except Rust and Python files. This is useful when you want to see all comments about work that needs to be done, but you're only interested in certain languages.

## Seeing All Available Types: `--type-list`

To see the complete list of file types that ripgrep knows about, run:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

This prints every type name, followed by a colon and the glob patterns that define it:

```
agda: *.agda
asm: *.asm, *.s
c: *.c, *.h
css: *.css, *.scss
rust: *.rs
```

Each type appears on its own line. The globs are comma-separated.

You can also filter this list to find a specific type. For example:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^web:'
```

## Defining Your Own File Types: `--type-add`

If ripgrep doesn't have a built-in type for what you're searching, you can create your own using `--type-add`. The syntax is `--type-add 'name:glob'`.

Suppose you frequently search "web" files—JavaScript, HTML, and CSS:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

This defines a new type called `web` and immediately applies it to the search. The search looks for the pattern `title` only in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files.

You can add multiple glob patterns to the same type by using multiple `--type-add` flags:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

Or combine them in one flag using glob syntax:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

When you run `--type-list` with a `--type-add` flag, your custom type shows up in the output, even though it's not part of ripgrep's built-in types.

## Important: Type Definitions Don't Persist

The `--type-add` flag only applies to the current command. Once the search finishes, your custom type is forgotten. If you want a type to be available in every ripgrep command, you have two options.

**Option 1: Use a shell alias**

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

**Option 2: Add it to a configuration file**

ripgrep supports a configuration file (usually `~/.config/ripgrep/config` or `.ripgreprc` in your project directory). You can put `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` in there, and ripgrep will apply it to every search. See the guide's section on configuration files for details.

## The Special `all` Type

ripgrep recognizes a special type name: `all`. Using `--type all` tells ripgrep to search only files that match *any* of the built-in types. This is a whitelist mode—ripgrep will only search recognized file types and skip everything else.

```
$ rg 'TODO' --type all
```

Similarly, `--type-not all` is a blacklist mode. It searches *only* files that ripgrep doesn't recognize:

```
$ rg 'TODO' --type-not all
```

This is useful when you want to find patterns in unusual or undocumented file formats that ripgrep doesn't have built-in types for.

## Combining With Other Filters

File type filtering works alongside ripgrep's other features. By default, ripgrep still respects your `.gitignore` files, skips hidden files and directories, and doesn't search binary files. The `--type` flag narrows things down even further.

File type filters also work with glob patterns (`-g`), though `--type` is often simpler for built-in types. And they work with every search pattern—regex, literal, or multiline.

## Practical Examples

**Find Python imports in your project:**
```
$ rg '^import ' --type python
```

**Search JavaScript but not in node_modules:**
```
$ rg --type javascript node_modules
```

**Look for SQL mistakes in a mixed codebase, excluding test files:**
```
$ rg 'SELCT' --type sql
```

**Search web templates for a particular class name:**
```
$ rg --type-add 'templates:*.jinja' --type-add 'templates:*.erb' -ttemplates 'hero-section'
```

File type filtering saves time and keeps your search results focused on what actually matters for the work you're doing.
